title: Biologic Therapies: Targets, Risks and the Lab Tests That Guard Them
summary: Learn what TNF blockers, natalizumab and vedolizumab, anakinra, tocilizumab, denosumab and the asthma biologics block, the risk each block creates, and the lab test that goes with it: latent TB screening, the anti-JC virus antibody index, eosinophil counts and a CRP that may stay low.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 49 Hits 7, 8, 10 and 11 and Traps 1 and 2, checked against Thaler 2009, Kucharz 2021, Faustman 2025, Shim 2014, McGuigan 2016, Glenn 2025, Colombel 2017, Card 2018, Luzentales-Simpson 2021, Mihara 2011, Koike 2009, Zhang 2020 and Gyawali 2025. Two qualifications are recorded: natalizumab binds the α4 chain shared by α4β1 and α4β7 (the reviewer says “anti-α4/β1”), and benralizumab binds the IL-5 receptor α rather than IL-5 itself (the reviewer groups it with the “anti-IL-5 drugs”). Not taught as fact: TNF inhibitors in juvenile arthritis, denosumab for tumour osteolysis, PML reports with vedolizumab after 2018. Lab content (IGRA, anti-JCV index, eosinophil thresholds, CRP masking) is added from the sources.

objectives: Name the target of TNF blockers, natalizumab, vedolizumab, anakinra, tocilizumab, denosumab, mepolizumab, reslizumab, benralizumab and dupilumab.
Link TNF blockade to tuberculosis and demyelination, and natalizumab to PML, and explain why vedolizumab differs.
Choose and interpret the lab test that goes with each drug: IGRA, anti-JC virus antibody index, eosinophil count, and CRP under tocilizumab.

scenes.title: Three biologics, three lab requests
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three patients are about to start biologic drugs and three requests reach the lab — (1) a patient with Crohn disease starting infliximab: interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA); (2) a patient with relapsing MS considering natalizumab: anti-JC virus (JCV) antibody index; (3) a patient with severe asthma being assessed for an IL-5 pathway drug: blood eosinophil count. Question token: “Why does the drug decide the test?”

cues.text: Three patients are about to start biologic drugs. A patient with Crohn disease is starting infliximab, and the lab receives an interferon-gamma release assay.
A patient with multiple sclerosis is considering natalizumab: the request is an anti-JC virus antibody index. A patient with severe asthma needs a blood eosinophil count.
Why does the drug decide which test the lab runs?

props.label: Why does the drug decide the test?

scenes.title: What each biologic blocks
scenes.altText: Schematic target map, four cards. TNF-α blockers: adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab, infliximab — dosed for RA, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, plaque psoriasis, Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Anti-integrins: natalizumab binds the α4 chain shared by α4β1 (binds VCAM-1; brain entry) and α4β7; vedolizumab binds only α4β7 (binds MAdCAM-1 on gut vessels), so it is gut-selective. Interleukin and RANKL blockers: anakinra = recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist (RA); tocilizumab binds soluble and membrane IL-6 receptor; denosumab binds RANKL and reduces osteoclast bone resorption. Asthma biologics: mepolizumab and reslizumab bind IL-5; benralizumab binds IL-5 receptor α and depletes eosinophils by ADCC; dupilumab binds IL-4 receptor α, blocking IL-4 and IL-13 signalling.

cues.text: Start with the targets. Five drugs block tumour necrosis factor: adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab and infliximab. They are used in rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriasis, Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.

Natalizumab binds the alpha-4 chain, so it blocks both alpha-4 beta-1, the integrin that lets cells enter the brain, and alpha-4 beta-7. Vedolizumab binds only alpha-4 beta-7, which steers lymphocytes into the gut.
Anakinra is a recombinant interleukin-1 receptor antagonist used in rheumatoid arthritis. Tocilizumab binds the interleukin-6 receptor. Denosumab binds RANKL and reduces osteoclast bone resorption.

In asthma, mepolizumab and reslizumab bind interleukin-5 itself, while benralizumab binds the interleukin-5 receptor and depletes eosinophils. Dupilumab binds the interleukin-4 receptor alpha chain, blocking interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling.

scenes.title: What blocking the signal costs
scenes.altText: Four risk cards. TNF blockade: increased risk of tuberculosis, mostly by reactivation of latent infection; demyelination (estimated 0.03–0.2% of treated patients) — the TNF inhibitor lenercept worsened MS in a trial, all anti-TNF drugs carry a warning and are avoided in suspected or diagnosed MS. Natalizumab: progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) from JC virus; risk highest with anti-JCV antibodies + any prior immunosuppressant + more than 24 months of therapy. Vedolizumab: no PML cases in its clinical development programme, although an average of six to seven would have been expected had the risk matched natalizumab’s. Tocilizumab: IL-6 drives CRP, so blocking it can hide fever, CRP and ESR rises during infection.

cues.text: Each block has a cost. Tumour necrosis factor blockers raise the risk of tuberculosis, mostly by reactivating latent infection. They can also trigger demyelination, estimated in 0.03 to 0.2 percent of treated patients.
The TNF inhibitor lenercept made multiple sclerosis worse in a trial, so the whole class carries a warning and is avoided in suspected or diagnosed multiple sclerosis.

Natalizumab reduces immune surveillance of the brain, which is thought to let JC virus cause progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Risk is highest with anti-JC virus antibodies, any prior immunosuppressant, and more than two years of treatment.
Vedolizumab stays in the gut: no cases were seen in its clinical trials, where six to seven would have been expected at natalizumab’s rate.
And interleukin-6 drives C-reactive protein, so tocilizumab can hide fever and the rise in C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate during an infection.

props.title: TNF blockers
lines: Avoid in suspected or known MS

props.label: Tocilizumab: CRP, ESR and fever can stay quiet in infection

scenes.title: The safety tests in the lab
scenes.altText: Three lab cards. Latent TB before anti-TNF: most organisations recommend screening before starting; IGRAs detect cell-mediated interferon-γ responses to M. tuberculosis antigens — QuantiFERON measures released IFN-γ by ELISA, T-SPOT.TB counts IFN-γ-secreting cells; one review suggests considering both TST and IGRA. Anti-JCV antibody: ELISA; the index is the sample optical density normalised to a calibrator; one review’s bands: <0.4 negative, 0.4–0.9 low, 0.9–1.5 medium, >1.5 high risk; a reported false-negative rate of about 2.5% and seroconversion mean negatives are retested (the EMA’s CHMP recommends six-monthly testing, as reported by a UK/Ireland expert group). Eosinophils: mepolizumab trials enrolled patients with blood eosinophils ≥150/µL at screening or ≥300/µL in the prior year, and reslizumab trials used ≥400/µL; dupilumab can cause a transient treatment-emergent eosinophilia (4% in one trial). Hook answers: IGRA for infliximab; anti-JCV index for natalizumab; eosinophil count for an IL-5 pathway drug.

cues.text: Before a TNF blocker starts, latent tuberculosis is screened for. Interferon-gamma release assays detect cell-mediated interferon-gamma responses to tuberculosis antigens: QuantiFERON measures the interferon by ELISA, and T-SPOT counts the secreting cells.

For natalizumab, an ELISA detects anti-JC virus antibodies, and the index is the sample’s optical density divided by a calibrator. One review bands it: below 0.4 negative, up to 0.9 low, up to 1.5 medium, above 1.5 high risk. Negatives are retested, because seroconversion and false negatives happen.

For interleukin-5 drugs, the mepolizumab trials enrolled blood eosinophils of at least 150 per microlitre at screening, or 300 in the previous year; reslizumab trials used 400. Dupilumab can cause a temporary rise in eosinophils.
So the drug decides the test: interferon-gamma release assay for infliximab, the JC virus antibody index for natalizumab, and an eosinophil count for an interleukin-5 pathway drug.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “TNF blockers suit any inflammatory disease” (✓ avoided in suspected or diagnosed MS; class warning after lenercept worsened MS); “Natalizumab and vedolizumab carry the same PML risk” (✓ natalizumab blocks α4β1 brain entry and carries PML risk; gut-selective vedolizumab had no PML cases in trials); “All three IL-5 drugs bind IL-5” (✓ benralizumab binds the IL-5 receptor α and depletes eosinophils).

cues.text: Trap one: TNF blockers suit any inflammatory disease. No: they are avoided in suspected or diagnosed multiple sclerosis, which lenercept made worse.
Trap two: both anti-integrins carry the same PML risk. No: natalizumab blocks brain entry and carries the risk; gut-selective vedolizumab had no cases in trials.
Trap three: all three interleukin-5 drugs bind interleukin-5. No: benralizumab binds the receptor and removes eosinophils.

scenes.title: Every block casts a shadow
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Every block casts a shadow, and the lab watches the shadow: TNF → TB, natalizumab → JC virus, IL-5 → eosinophils, IL-6 → a silent CRP.” Four tokens. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: every block casts a shadow, and the lab watches the shadow. Tumour necrosis factor casts tuberculosis. Natalizumab casts JC virus. Interleukin-5 casts the eosinophil count. Interleukin-6 casts a silent C-reactive protein.

Where it breaks: each drug has other risks and tests; index cut-offs belong to a specific assay; a negative JC virus antibody is not zero risk; and the eosinophil numbers were trial entry criteria, not universal cut-offs.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “TNF blocker → latent TB screen · avoid in MS”, “Natalizumab → anti-JCV index · IL-5 drugs → eosinophils · tocilizumab → CRP may stay low”.

cues.text: Match each biologic to its safety test: latent tuberculosis screening before tumour necrosis factor blockers, which are avoided in multiple sclerosis, the anti-JC virus antibody index for natalizumab, and eosinophil counts for interleukin-5 pathway drugs, remembering that tocilizumab can keep C-reactive protein low during infection.

props.label: TNF blocker → latent TB screen · avoid in MS
Natalizumab → anti-JCV index · IL-5 → eosinophils · IL-6 → low CRP

explanation.what: Plain language: biologics are engineered proteins that block one immune signal or one door that white cells use. Blocking a signal also removes some of its protective work, so each drug comes with a predictable risk and a lab test to watch for it. Scientific terms: tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) inhibitor, α4β1 and α4β7 integrins, VCAM-1, MAdCAM-1, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), JC virus (JCV), IL-1 receptor antagonist, IL-6 receptor, RANKL, IL-5 receptor α (IL-5Rα), IL-4 receptor α (IL-4Rα), antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), interferon-γ release assay (IGRA).
explanation.why: Patients on TNF blockers are at increased risk of tuberculosis, mostly through reactivation of latent infection; demyelination is a rare class effect, and the TNF inhibitor lenercept worsened MS. Natalizumab binds the α4 chain and so blocks α4β1–VCAM-1 entry of lymphocytes into the brain, which lets JC virus cause PML; vedolizumab binds only α4β7, the gut-homing integrin that binds MAdCAM-1. IL-6 drives CRP production, so blocking its receptor can keep CRP and ESR low during infection.
explanation.measure: Before anti-TNF: latent TB screening (IGRA: QuantiFERON measures IFN-γ by ELISA, T-SPOT.TB counts IFN-γ-secreting cells; a TST may be added). Natalizumab: anti-JCV antibody ELISA; index = sample optical density normalised to a calibrator; one review’s bands: < 0.4 negative, 0.4–0.9 low, 0.9–1.5 medium, > 1.5 high risk; repeat testing in negatives (the EMA’s CHMP recommends six-monthly anti-JCV testing, as reported by a UK/Ireland expert group); the index bands are used to stratify immunosuppressant-naive patients. PML risk is highest with antibody positivity + any prior immunosuppressant + > 24 months of therapy. Mepolizumab trials enrolled blood eosinophils ≥ 150/µL at screening or ≥ 300/µL in the prior year; reslizumab trials used ≥ 400/µL. Dupilumab can cause a transient treatment-emergent eosinophilia.
explanation.differs: Natalizumab (α4 chain: α4β1 + α4β7; brain and gut) vs vedolizumab (α4β7 only; gut). Mepolizumab and reslizumab (bind IL-5) vs benralizumab (binds IL-5Rα, depletes eosinophils by ADCC). Dupilumab blocks the IL-4Rα chain shared by the IL-4 and IL-13 receptor complexes. Anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) vs tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor) vs denosumab (RANKL).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the drug contraindicated in MS (TNF blockers), the anti-integrin with PML risk (natalizumab), the pre-treatment lab test (IGRA, anti-JCV antibody), the biologic that blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 (dupilumab), or a low CRP in a febrile patient on tocilizumab.

questions.stem: A patient with MS has received natalizumab for 30 months, previously received mitoxantrone, and has an anti-JCV antibody index of 2.1. How is the PML risk best described?

options.text: In the highest-risk group: antibody positive, prior immunosuppressant and more than 24 months of therapy
options.rationale: Correct. Antibody positivity, any prior immunosuppressant and more than 24 months of therapy together mark the highest-risk group; the index bands are used mainly to stratify immunosuppressant-naive patients.

options.text: Negligible, because the index is a qualitative test
options.rationale: Incorrect. The index is a normalised optical density; higher values carry higher risk.

options.text: Low, because the risk falls after the first 2 years
options.rationale: Incorrect. Risk rises after 24 months of exposure.
Incorrect. Any prior immunosuppressant use is a recognised PML risk factor.

questions.stem: Which asthma biologic binds the IL-5 receptor α chain rather than IL-5 itself?

options.rationale: Correct. It binds IL-5Rα and depletes eosinophils by antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity.
Incorrect. Mepolizumab binds the IL-5 ligand.
Incorrect. Reslizumab also binds the IL-5 ligand.
Incorrect. Dupilumab binds IL-4Rα, blocking IL-4 and IL-13 signalling.

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis receiving tocilizumab has a cough and malaise, but a normal CRP. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Blocking the IL-6 receptor can suppress CRP, so a normal CRP does not exclude infection
options.rationale: Correct. IL-6 drives CRP production, and tocilizumab can mask fever, CRP and ESR rises.

options.text: Infection is excluded because CRP is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Tocilizumab can suppress CRP and ESR rises, so CRP is unreliable for excluding infection; cough itself is not masked.

options.text: The CRP assay must be faulty
options.rationale: Incorrect. Suppressed CRP is a recognised drug effect, not evidence of assay failure.

options.text: The normal CRP shows tocilizumab has stopped working
options.rationale: Incorrect. A normal CRP is consistent with the drug acting on IL-6 signalling.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 49 Hit 8 calls natalizumab “anti-α4/β1”. Natalizumab binds the α4 chain shared by α4β1 and α4β7 (Luzentales-Simpson 2021; Glenn 2025); its PML risk is attributed to α4β1 blockade of brain entry. “No PML in trials” for vedolizumab is time-bound to the 2017–2018 reports (register flag rv-natalizumab-alpha4-chain).

Ch. 49 Hit 11 lists benralizumab among “anti-IL-5 drugs”. Gyawali 2025: mepolizumab and reslizumab bind IL-5, but benralizumab binds IL-5Rα and depletes eosinophils by ADCC; dupilumab’s sinus indication is chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (register flag rv-benralizumab-il5-receptor).
